question: Can real-space mutual-information compression discover locally appropriate collective variables on inhomogeneous static graphs, and does applying it to Ammann-Beenker dimers reveal a discrete-scale-invariant super-dimer theory?

key_findings.claim: The paper makes the RSMI variational principle computationally usable on a fixed irregular graph by optimizing a separate local compressor against a distant environment.
key_findings.evidence: For each block V at location or vertex class i, a binary coarse variable H=T(A_i V) is chosen to maximize mutual information with a graph-distance-separated environment E. Mutual information is replaced by a contrastive neural lower bound that distinguishes joint from product-of-marginals samples. A fixed vertex labeling converts static-graph configurations to vectors, allowing ordinary linear or nonlinear networks rather than a permutation-equivariant graph model.

key_findings.claim: On the Ammann-Beenker dimer ensemble, the learned encodings recover structured local clock variables rather than arbitrary bit clusters.
key_findings.evidence: The retained-information curve saturates at four binary components for an 8-supervertex block and two for a 3-supervertex. Only eight of sixteen class-8 codes occur, each with probability 1/8 and arranged in a one-bit Hamming cycle; local C8 rotations permute filters and move between neighboring codes. The three used class-3 codes transform under the block's mirror symmetry. These relations support identifying codes with orientations of Z8 and Z3 clock variables.

key_findings.claim: Conditional correlations at two even deflation scales give strong evidence that learned clocks bind into emergent super-dimers.
key_findings.evidence: At delta-squared and delta-to-the-fourth super-quasilattices, conditioning one clock direction sharply selects a matching neighbor and excludes competing matches, reproducing the microscopic one-dimer-per-vertex constraint and longer-range patterns. Filters at the largest displayed scale act on 2,760 microscopic links. Graph-distance-defined blocks reproduce the same clock and exclusion structures, so the result is not tied to one polygonal block boundary.

key_findings.claim: The phrase 'demonstrating DSI' is stronger than the learned analysis alone: the scale hierarchy is supplied in advance and no RG fixed-point flow is estimated.
key_findings.evidence: Blocks are centered on known Ammann-Beenker supervertices, chosen from known inflated tiles or graph radii selected to correspond to known deflations, and evaluated specifically at delta-squared and delta-to-the-fourth scales. The method recovers analogous clocks and conditional exclusion at those scales and an even/odd alternation in its learned mutual-information bound. It does not discover the silver-ratio scale factor, infer the coarse graph from raw connectivity, fit effective couplings, show their convergence under repeated transformation, estimate scaling dimensions, or test log-periodic observables. An independent exact decimation construction cited by the paper supplies the stronger fixed-point result.

key_findings.claim: Bit-count saturation can reflect the critic and encoder geometry as well as intrinsic physical cardinality, but estimator bias is not calibrated.
key_findings.evidence: The optimized objective is a lower bound from a fixed separable critic u(H)^T v(E), not mutual information itself. The code dimension is selected where this trained bound plateaus after Gumbel-softmax annealing, 120 epochs, and repeated optimization. No synthetic problem with known latent cardinality, held-out lower-bound evaluation, critic-capacity sweep, alternative MI estimator, or confidence interval for the main bit plateaus is reported. The later 2026 literature specifically finds separable/bilinear neural critics can systematically inflate inferred task-relevant dimension.

key_findings.claim: The claimed arbitrary-geometry scope is real but substantially narrower than arbitrary dynamical or globally consistent coarse graining.
key_findings.evidence: The vectorization trick requires a static graph and a fixed coordinate labeling; the paper explicitly says it cannot handle dynamic graphs this way. Local relevance also depends on a chosen block, environment shell, and buffer screening short-range correlations. Independently trained local maps retain sign or code-permutation gauge freedom; the random-graph Z2 example needs overlapping blocks and manual sign stitching. General multi-state stitching, emergent connectivity, effective couplings, chart changes, graph shortcuts, long-range interactions, varying topology, and out-of-ensemble transfer are not solved.

key_findings.claim: The supplementary Max-Cut comparison does not establish superiority to Goemans-Williamson or a certified approximation ratio.
key_findings.evidence: RSMI-NE is tested on easy, nearly bipartite planted planar-derived graphs and compared with random cuts and greedy one-exchange. The denominator called the optimum is the local-search cut, even though that heuristic has no global guarantee. Goemans-Williamson is not run; its 0.878 worst-case guarantee is drawn as a horizontal line. Achieving a larger empirical ratio on this easy ensemble is not outperforming that algorithm, and RSMI-NE drops toward the line as frustration rises. Runtime includes one reused 1,804-node Monte Carlo sample source and only hundreds-node instances, so scaling and solution quality remain provisional.

method.core_idea: Define relevance locally by the information a compressed block retains about a spatially separated environment, letting the data rather than translational symmetry select collective degrees of freedom.
method.mechanism: A local linear filter maps graph-labeled configurations to a few logits, Gumbel-softmax produces capacity-limited binary codes, and a bilinear neural critic supplies a differentiable contrastive lower bound on block-environment mutual information. Separate maps are trained by block class or location, then their code symmetries and cross-block conditional distributions are interpreted as emergent variables and interactions.
assumptions: A graph-distance buffer removes irrelevant local correlations while preserving the long-range signal of interest.
The sampled equilibrium ensemble is representative and sufficiently mixed.
The chosen neural lower bound preserves the ordering and saturation of true mutual information across encoders and bit counts.
A fixed graph labeling is stable and physically meaningful enough for vector-valued networks.
Local compressors can be gauge-aligned into a globally coherent coarse theory.
The selected block centers and scales do not inject the target emergent structure.
Repeating conditional structures at selected scales is adequate evidence for the intended scale invariance.

techniques.role: Selects a compressed variable by maximizing information with a distant graph environment.
Estimates a variational MI lower bound through joint-versus-shuffled-pair classification.
Enforces a fixed binary information rate while retaining gradient-based training.
Applies known local rotations or reflections to identify learned codes with clock states.
Uses conditional code distributions to infer super-dimer exclusion and effective edges.
Aligns signs of overlapping independently trained Z2 filters into a global order parameter.

evaluations.setting: Close-packed dimers on a 26,177-node Ammann-Beenker graph, using 50,000 directed-loop Monte Carlo configurations and 120 training epochs.
evaluations.metric: Variational RSMI lower bound versus bit count, code occupancy, filter symmetry, and conditional code distributions.
evaluations.result: Four-bit/eight-state and two-bit/three-state clocks emerge for 8- and 3-supervertices and transform consistently with local spatial symmetries.
evaluations.baseline: Different code capacities and nonlinear compressors; no alternative MI estimator or ground-truth latent benchmark.

evaluations.setting: Known even Ammann-Beenker deflations at delta-squared and delta-to-the-fourth, plus odd deflations in the supplement.
evaluations.metric: Persistence of clock codes, learned MI, and microscopic-versus-coarse conditional dimer correlations.
evaluations.result: Even scales reproduce super-dimer exclusion and longer correlations; odd scales have roughly half the learned MI and lack clear three-state clusters across five optimization runs.
evaluations.baseline: Microscopic dimer conditional probabilities and adjacent odd/even selected scales.

evaluations.setting: Alternative graph-distance blocks centered on known Ammann-Beenker supervertices.
evaluations.result: The same clock interpretation and matching direction are recovered, supporting robustness to block boundary shape.

evaluations.setting: Antiferromagnetic Ising configurations on nearly bipartite random planar-derived graphs with 0-7.5% edge frustration.
evaluations.metric: MI bit saturation, bimodality, stitched magnetization, correlation, cut per edge, and runtime.
evaluations.result: A one-bit filter recovers the planted bipartition through modest frustration, yields a global order parameter, and produces cuts near greedy one-exchange on the selected ensemble.
evaluations.baseline: Random partition, greedy local one-exchange, and a plotted Goemans-Williamson worst-case guarantee rather than an executed GW solver.

limitations: Main DSI experiments use known supervertices, known deflation scales, and scale-matched blocks rather than discovering the hierarchy from an unstructured graph.
No effective-Hamiltonian couplings, RG flow, fixed point, scaling dimensions, or log-periodic observable are learned.
The neural MI lower bound and bit saturation are not calibrated against known ground truth or alternative critics.
There is no explicit held-out split or generalization analysis for the 50,000 Monte Carlo configurations.
The graph must be static and assigned a fixed vertex coordinate ordering.
Block, buffer, and environment radii remain expert choices and may fail with graph shortcuts or long-range interactions.
Independent local maps have unresolved gauge/permutation consistency beyond the demonstrated Z2 stitching.
The random-graph study is an easy nearly bipartite ensemble at hundreds-node scale and does not run certified Max-Cut baselines.
Most uncertainty is optimization variability; Monte Carlo, finite-size, block-choice, and model-selection uncertainty are not comprehensively propagated.
failure_modes: The critic saturates, causing a false plateau that under- or over-estimates the number of relevant variables.
A too-small buffer encodes local constraints rather than emergent long-range physics.
A too-large environment makes contrastive estimation sample-inefficient or learns graph identity artifacts.
Fixed vertex labels let filters exploit arbitrary indexing and fail under relabeling.
Local clock gauges cannot be aligned consistently around loops, preventing a global coarse theory.
Known block centers leak the desired inflation hierarchy into an apparent discovery.
Monte Carlo autocorrelation or incomplete mixing distorts learned mutual information.
Increasing frustration mixes several slow observables, so a one-bit compressor ceases to represent Max-Cut or AFM order.
reusable_insights: Use a separated environment to define relevance without relying on wavelength or translation invariance.
Inspect the transformation law of learned filters under physical symmetries, not only their predictive score.
Treat code cardinality, code geometry, and number of binary hyperplanes as distinct quantities.
Test a learned coarse variable by whether it reproduces conditional constraints and long-range observables across scales.
Make local gauge alignment an explicit optimization problem when independently learned variables form a global field.
Benchmark MI-based dimension selection on synthetic latent systems and multiple critic families before using plateaus as physical evidence.
Compare executed algorithms and certified optima or bounds; an empirical score above another method's worst-case guarantee is not a head-to-head win.
open_questions: Can the blocks, scale factor, coarse connectivity, and local cardinalities be discovered jointly from an unlabeled graph ensemble?
Can permutation-equivariant compressors extend RSMI-NE to dynamic, relabeled, or varying-topology graphs?
How can multi-state local gauges be synchronized with uncertainty and obstruction detection?
Will a richer critic change the inferred four-bit and two-bit saturation points?
Can learned clocks produce a quantitative effective Hamiltonian whose couplings demonstrably flow to the exact dimer fixed point?
Which buffer conditions guarantee that maximizing distant MI selects RG-relevant operators on irregular graphs with long-range edges?
How does the method compare with spectral, Laplacian, harmonic-morphism, geometric, and message-passing coarse grainings on common real networks?

competitive_landscape.title: Discrete scale invariant fixed point in a quasiperiodic classical dimer model
competitive_landscape.difference: Biswas and Parameswaran explicitly construct the exact decimation, fit nonzero dimer potentials, show flow to a fixed-point Hamiltonian, and derive slow correlations; it provides stronger DSI evidence while relying on more analytic system knowledge than the learned compressor.

competitive_landscape.title: Renormalization Group-Motivated Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Landy et al. select pairs and balance local correlation against global projection error, extending to mutual information for nonlinear data; it offers an alternative route to collective features without the paper's fixed block-environment construction.

competitive_landscape.title: Mutual Information and Task-Relevant Latent Dimensionality
competitive_landscape.difference: Gulati et al. show separable/bilinear neural critics can systematically inflate inferred latent dimension, introduce a hybrid critic, and validate on known-dimensional synthetic data, directly challenging uncalibrated bit-plateau inference.

competitive_landscape.title: Multiscale network renormalization: scale-invariance without geometry
competitive_landscape.difference: Garuccio, Lalli, and Garlaschelli define a graph renormalization valid for heterogeneous block hierarchies and characterize model-level scale invariance on real networks, focusing on graph ensembles rather than physical variables living on a fixed graph.

competitive_landscape.title: Harmonic morphisms and dynamical invariants in network renormalization
competitive_landscape.difference: Guadagnuolo et al. give a minimal condition for exactly preserving random-walk dynamics plus a harmonic-degree diagnostic across geometric, Laplacian, and GNN coarse grainings, supplying quantitative validation criteria beyond retained MI.

competitive_landscape.title: Dreaming up scale invariance via inverse renormalization group
competitive_landscape.difference: Rancon et al. learn an inverse map with extremely small networks and validate it through susceptibilities, heat capacity, Binder ratios, and nontrivial RG eigenvalues, emphasizing quantitative scale-invariant observables rather than code interpretation.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Compression theory and RSMI-NE overcome translational invariance by learning different relevant variables locally on arbitrary graphs; on Ammann-Beenker dimers they expose clock variables and self-similar super-dimers, and on frustrated random graphs they recover an AFM order parameter and near-optimal bipartition.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The work extends a public RSMI implementation to static NetworkX graphs, learns distinct code lengths and symmetry representations, reproduces conditional dimer exclusion across two even scales and alternate block shapes, and supplies a random-graph demonstration with gauge stitching.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Learning interpretable, location-dependent coarse variables on an irregular graph is a substantive contribution, and the clock-code symmetry analysis is unusually human-readable. The DSI hierarchy is partly supplied by known Ammann-Beenker structure, the learned analysis stops short of an RG fixed point, MI dimension selection is estimator-dependent, and the Max-Cut comparison overclaims an unexecuted worst-case baseline. Exact, estimator-calibrated, and dynamics-preserving competitors now define stronger tests.

reviewer_notes: Read all 18 OCR-extracted pages, including the full supplement and references. Visually inspected main Figures 1-4 and Supplementary Figures 1-10; figures confirm the known scale/block construction, two even learned scales, five-run MI error bars only for the odd/even comparison, Z2 gauge stitching, and the use of the Goemans-Williamson guarantee rather than solver outputs. Six primary arXiv/PMLR competitors were checked on 2026-08-23.
